p.src: When dawn broke, the monks found that Tripitaka and his disciples had disappeared. They all said, “We did not manage to keep them, bid them farewell, or make our entreaties; we simply let a living bodhisattva slip away.” While they were speaking, several wealthy householders from the southern suburb arrived to invite the pilgrims. The monks clapped their hands and said, “We failed to keep watch last night, and this very night they all rode away on clouds.” The visitors all faced the sky and bowed in gratitude. Once this tale was told, every official and inhabitant in the city soon heard of it. The wealthy families were instructed to prepare offerings of the five sacrificial animals, flowers, and fruit, and to present them at the shrine built in the pilgrims’ honor in repayment of their grace. Of this we shall say no more.

p.src: Meanwhile, the Tang monk and his three companions journeyed on, dining in the wind and sleeping beside the waters. All was peaceful along the road, and more than half a month passed. Then one day, they saw a lofty mountain. Once more the Tang monk grew afraid and said, “Disciple, the ridges ahead are steep and rugged. We must be careful.” Pilgrim laughed. “We are drawing near the Buddha’s land. There can certainly be no fiends or evil spirits here. Set your mind at ease, Master, and do not worry.” The Tang monk said, “Disciple, though the Buddha’s land is not far away, the monks at that monastery said the capital of India was still two thousand li distant. We do not yet know how much farther we must travel.” Pilgrim said, “Master, surely you have forgotten the Heart Sutra taught to you by the Crow’s Nest Chan Master again.” Tripitaka said, “The Heart Sutra is the robe and bowl I carry always with me. Since the Crow’s Nest Chan Master taught it to me, has a single day passed when I did not recite it? When have I ever forgotten it? I can recite it even backward—how could I possibly forget it?” Pilgrim said, “Master, you can recite it, but you never sought the master’s explanation of it.” Tripitaka said, “You ape, why do you say again that I do not understand it? Do you understand it, then?” Pilgrim replied, “I understand it. I understand it.” After that, neither Tripitaka nor Pilgrim spoke another word. At their side, Eight Rules doubled over with laughter, while Sha Monk was highly amused. Eight Rules said, “Longmouth, he started life as a monster just as I did. He is no Chan monk who has listened to sermons, nor has he ever seen an eminent Buddhist master expounding the Dharma. He is only putting on airs and making a show of himself, talking about how he ‘knows’ and ‘understands.’ Why has he suddenly fallen silent? Let us hear him explain it.” Sha Monk said, “Second Brother, do you really believe him? Elder Brother was merely spinning out the conversation to coax Master onward. He knows how to wield his cudgel, that is all. How would he know how to expound a sutra?” Tripitaka said, “Wuneng, Wujing, do not talk nonsense. Wukong’s understanding is beyond speech and writing; that is true understanding.”

p.src: Pilgrim read the name as “Gold-Spreading Chan Monastery,” and Eight Rules likewise said it was the “Gold-Spreading Chan Monastery.” Sitting on his horse, Tripitaka pondered aloud, “‘Spreading gold’… ‘spreading gold’… Can this be the territory of Shravasti?” Eight Rules said, “Master, how strange! I have followed you for years without ever seeing you recognize the road. Have you learned your way around today?” Tripitaka said, “That is not it. I often read and recite the scriptures, which say that the Buddha stayed at Prince Jeta’s Grove in the Garden of Anathapindika at the city of Shravasti. It is said that the Elder Anathapindika sought to buy this garden from the prince so that he might invite the Buddha to preach. The prince said, ‘My garden is not for sale. If he wishes to buy it, he must first cover its entire ground with gold.’ When the Elder Anathapindika heard this, he had gold made into bricks and spread them over the whole garden. Only then did he acquire Prince Jeta’s grove and invite the World-Honored One to expound the Dharma. I wonder whether this Gold-Spreading Monastery takes its name from that very story.” Eight Rules laughed. “What luck! If it is the same story, let us go and feel around for a brick or two to give away.” They all laughed for a while longer before Tripitaka finally dismounted.

p.src: When Tripitaka saw him, he saluted him. The monk hurriedly returned the courtesy and asked, “From where have you come, Master?” Tripitaka replied, “This disciple is Chen Xuanzang. By command of the emperor of the Great Tang in the Eastern Land, I have been sent to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures. Passing through your honored region, I have ventured to pay my respects and ask lodging for one night. We shall leave tomorrow.” The monk said, “This poor mountain monastery belongs to the whole Buddhist community, and all visitors are welcome to share its hospitality. All the more so when you are a holy monk from the Eastern Land. It would be our great good fortune merely to make offerings to you.” Tripitaka thanked him and immediately called his three disciples to follow. They passed the cloister and the monastery kitchen, then went straight into the abbot’s quarters. After exchanging courtesies, host and guests took their appointed seats. Pilgrim and the other two also sat down respectfully, their hands lowered at their sides.

p.src: Word now spread through the monastery that a scripture-seeking monk from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land had arrived. Everyone there, high and low—resident monks, visiting monks, elders, and novices alike—came one by one to pay their respects. When tea was finished, a vegetarian meal was set out. While the elder was still chanting the verse before the meal, the impatient Eight Rules was already gulping down steamed buns, vegetarian dishes, and vermicelli soup all together. The abbot’s quarters were crowded by then. Those of discernment praised Tripitaka’s dignified bearing, while those who enjoyed a spectacle watched Eight Rules eat. Sha Monk glanced around and saw every eye fixed on them. Secretly he pinched Eight Rules and said, “Mind your manners.” Eight Rules grew flustered and cried out in agitation, “Manners, manners—but my belly is empty!” Sha Monk laughed. “Second Brother, you do not understand. There are many refined gentlemen in the world, but if we speak of what lies inside their bellies, they are just the same as you and me.” Only then did Eight Rules agree to stop. Tripitaka recited the closing grace. The attendants cleared away the dishes, and Tripitaka offered his thanks.

p.src: When the monks asked why they had come from the Eastern Land, Tripitaka recounted their journey through ancient sites, then asked how the Temple of Gold-Paved Ground had received its name. The monk replied, “This temple was originally Anathapindika’s Jetavana Monastery in the kingdom of Shravasti, also called Jeta Grove. Because the elder Anathapindika invited the Buddha to preach here and covered the ground with gold bricks, it later acquired its present name. Within sight before our temple lies the kingdom of Shravasti. At that time the elder Anathapindika lived in Shravasti, and this barren mountain was once his Jeta Grove; hence it came to be called Anathapindika’s Temple of Gold-Paved Ground. Behind the temple, the foundations of Jeta Grove still remain. In recent years, whenever torrential seasonal rains fall, they have even washed out little beads of gold and silver. Those blessed by fortune often find them.” Tripitaka said, “So the tale handed down is indeed true.” He asked again, “When we first entered this precious mountain, we saw many traveling merchants with mules, horses, carts, and loads beneath the two galleries by the gate. Why are they lodging here?” The monks said, “Our mountain is called Hundred-Leg Mountain. In former years it was entirely peaceful, but lately, with the turning of the seasons, several centipede demons have somehow appeared and often harm travelers on the road. Though they do not actually take lives, people truly dare not travel there. At the foot of the mountain stands a pass called Cockcrow Pass. Only when the cock crows do people dare pass through. Those travelers arrived late and feared trouble, so they have borrowed lodging on our barren mountain for one night and will depart after cockcrow.” Tripitaka said, “Then let us also wait until cockcrow before leaving.” As master and disciples were speaking, another vegetarian meal was brought, which the Tang monk and the others finished.

p.src: They all admired the moon as they walked slowly on. Near the rear gate they climbed onto a terrace and sat awhile, when suddenly they heard the sound of weeping. Tripitaka calmed his mind and listened closely; the weeper lamented that her father and mother knew nothing of her suffering. His heart was touched with sorrow, and tears fell unbidden. Turning to the monks, he asked, “Who is grieving so bitterly, and where?” At this question, the old monk ordered the other monks to return first and brew tea. When no one else remained, he bowed to the Tang monk and Pilgrim. Tripitaka helped him up and said, “Venerable abbot, why do you pay us such a courtesy?” The old monk said, “This disciple is over a hundred years old and knows something of worldly affairs. During meditative stillness, I have also witnessed visions several times. As for you, my lords, master and disciples, I know a little about you and understand that you are unlike other men. As for this sorrowful matter, none but this master here can discern its truth.” Pilgrim said, “Tell us, then. What is the matter?” The old monk said, “On this very day last year, while I was illuminating the moon of my true nature, I suddenly heard a gust of wind, followed by a voice of grief and resentment. I left my couch and went to inspect the foundations of Jeta Grove, where I found a beautiful and comely young woman. I asked her, ‘Whose daughter are you? Why have you come to this place?’ The young woman said, ‘I am the princess of the kingdom of India. While viewing flowers beneath the moon, I was swept here by the wind.’ I locked her in a dilapidated empty room, bricked it up to resemble a prison cell, and left only a small opening in the door, barely wide enough to pass a bowl through. That same day I told the other monks, ‘She is an evil spirit whom I have bound.’ Yet we monks are compassionate people and would not take her life. Each day we give her two meals of coarse tea and plain food to keep her alive. The young woman is clever and immediately understood my intention. Fearing she might be defiled by the monks, she pretends to be mad and acts grotesquely, sleeping in urine and lying in excrement. By day she talks nonsense and behaves like a witless fool. But in the stillness of night she thinks of her parents and weeps. Several times I went into the city to inquire about the princess, but found no news at all. For that reason I have kept her securely confined and never let her out. Now, by good fortune, you have come to this kingdom. I earnestly beg you, once you enter the capital, to exercise your great powers and investigate the truth: first, to rescue the innocent, and second, to manifest your divine abilities.” When Tripitaka and Pilgrim had heard him out, they took the matter deeply to heart.

p.src: They had not slept long that night when they heard the cock crow. Up ahead, all the traveling merchants rose in a bustling clamor, lit lamps, and prepared their meals. The elder also awakened Bajie and Sha Monk to saddle the horse and pack their things, while Pilgrim called for a lamp. The temple monks had risen even earlier and prepared tea, hot water, and refreshments, waiting respectfully in the rear. Delighted, Bajie ate a whole plate of steamed buns, then brought out the luggage and horse. Tripitaka and Pilgrim thanked everyone and took their leave. The old monk again said to Pilgrim, “Keep the sorrowful matter in mind—do keep it in mind.” Pilgrim laughed. “Your request is received, received with care. Once in the city, I shall know how to hear a voice and discern its meaning, to see a face and read its expression.” The band of traveling merchants also set out on the main road amid a noisy hubbub. Near the Hour of the Tiger, they passed through Cockcrow Pass. Only at the Hour of the Serpent did the city walls come into view. It was truly a city strong as an iron jar and walls of gold, a divine realm and celestial seat. The city was thus:

p.src: That day they entered the eastern market street, where the merchants each made for an inn. As master and disciples proceeded through the city, they came upon the official posthouse for foreign envoys, and Tripitaka and the others went straight inside. A steward in the posthouse immediately reported to the postmaster, “Four very strange-looking monks have come in from outside, leading a white horse.” Hearing that they had a horse, the postmaster knew they were on official business and came out of the hall to welcome them. Tripitaka saluted him and said, “This poor monk is an imperial envoy of the Tang court in the Eastern Land, traveling to Vulture Peak to see the Buddha at the Great Thunderclap Monastery and seek the scriptures. I carry a travel rescript that must be presented at court for inspection. We ask to rest awhile in your honorable offices and shall leave as soon as our business is done.” Returning the salute, the postmaster said, “This office was established precisely to receive envoys and travelers, so it is only proper that we entertain you. Please enter, please enter.” Tripitaka was delighted and told all his disciples to come forward and meet him. When the postmaster saw their hideous faces, he was secretly terrified, unable to tell whether they were men or ghosts. Trembling, he could only order tea and a vegetarian meal to be served. Seeing his fear, Tripitaka said, “My lord, do not be alarmed. Though my three disciples are ugly in appearance, all are good at heart. As the common saying goes, ‘An ugly face may hide a good man.’ Why should you be afraid?”

u.src: That day they entered the eastern market street, where the merchants each made for an inn.
As master and disciples proceeded through the city, they came upon the official posthouse for foreign envoys, and Tripitaka and the others went straight inside.
A steward in the posthouse immediately reported to the postmaster, “Four very strange-looking monks have come in from outside, leading a white horse.”
Hearing that they had a horse, the postmaster knew they were on official business and came out of the hall to welcome them.

Tripitaka saluted him and said, “This poor monk is an imperial envoy of the Tang court in the Eastern Land, traveling to Vulture Peak to see the Buddha at the Great Thunderclap Monastery and seek the scriptures. I carry a travel rescript that must be presented at court for inspection.
We ask to rest awhile in your honorable offices and shall leave as soon as our business is done.”
Returning the salute, the postmaster said, “This office was established precisely to receive envoys and travelers, so it is only proper that we entertain you.
Please enter, please enter.”
Tripitaka was delighted and told all his disciples to come forward and meet him.
When the postmaster saw their hideous faces, he was secretly terrified, unable to tell whether they were men or ghosts. Trembling, he could only order tea and a vegetarian meal to be served.
Seeing his fear, Tripitaka said, “My lord, do not be alarmed. Though my three disciples are ugly in appearance, all are good at heart.
As the common saying goes, ‘An ugly face may hide a good man.’ Why should you be afraid?”

p.src: Hearing this, the postmaster finally composed himself and asked, “Reverend Master, where does the Tang realm lie?” Tripitaka replied, “In the land of China, within the Southern Continent of Jambudvipa.” The postmaster asked again, “When did you leave home?” Tripitaka said, “In the thirteenth year of Zhenguan. Fourteen years have now passed, and only after painfully crossing countless rivers and mountains have I reached this place.” The postmaster exclaimed, “A holy monk indeed! A holy monk indeed!” Tripitaka asked, “How many years has your exalted kingdom endured?” The postmaster replied, “Our humble land is the Great Kingdom of India. From the founding emperor and his successor down to the present, more than five hundred years have passed. His present Majesty delights in mountains, waters, flowers, and plants, and is styled Emperor Yizong. He inaugurated the Jingyan era, now in its twenty-eighth year.” Tripitaka said, “Today I wish to have an audience and exchange my travel rescript. Do you know whether I may find the court in session?” The postmaster said, “Good, good—your timing is perfect. Our king’s princess recently reached the bloom of her twentieth year. A lofty festooned tower has been erected at the crossroads, from which she is casting an embroidered ball and leaving Heaven to choose her a consort. Today the festivities are at their height, so I expect His Majesty has not yet withdrawn from court. If you wish to exchange your rescript, now is the time to go.” Tripitaka gladly made ready to leave, but just then the vegetarian meal was set out, so he ate with the postmaster, Pilgrim, and the others.

p.src: By then it was already past noon. Tripitaka said, “I had better be going.” Pilgrim said, “I will go and protect Master.” Eight Rules said, “I’ll go.” Friar Sand said, “Forget it, Second Brother. Have you never looked at that face of yours? Don’t go showing off outside the palace gate. Let Eldest Brother go instead.” Tripitaka said, “Wujing speaks wisely. That Idiot is coarse and clumsy, while Wukong has some delicacy.” Pouting, the Idiot said, “Master aside, the three of us look much the same.” Tripitaka put on his cassock, while Pilgrim took the document pouch, and the two departed together. In the streets, scholars and farmers, artisans and merchants, men of letters, common fools, and ordinary folk were all clamoring, “Let’s go watch the embroidered ball being cast!” Tripitaka stopped by the roadside and said to Pilgrim, “The people and their dress here, their palaces and utensils, and even their speech and manners are all much like those of our Great Tang. It reminds me that my late mother, before she entered the religious life, also cast an embroidered ball, met the husband destined for her from former lives, and became his wife. They have the same custom here.” Pilgrim said, “Why don’t we go and have a look too?” Tripitaka said, “No, no. Our clothing makes that inadvisable; we might arouse suspicion.” Pilgrim said, “Master, have you forgotten what the old monk at the Gold-Spreading Monastery of the Solitary One told us? For one thing, we can see the festooned tower; for another, we can distinguish the true from the false. With such a commotion under way, the emperor will surely be waiting for news of the princess’s happy match. How could he be attending court and handling affairs? Let us go there first.” Persuaded by these words, Tripitaka accompanied Pilgrim and saw people of every sort gathered there to watch the embroidered ball being cast. Ah! Little did he know that this excursion would lead to this:

p.src: Now the king of India, being fond of mountains, waters, flowers, and plants, had taken his queen, consorts, and princess to admire the imperial garden by moonlight two years before. This stirred a fiend to action: it abducted the true princess and transformed itself into a false one. Knowing the very year, month, day, and hour when the Tang Monk would arrive, the fiend used the kingdom’s wealth to erect the festooned tower. It meant to take him as a mate, absorb the pure primal yang of his vital essence, and thereby become an immortal of the Supreme Unity.

Knowing the very year, month, day, and hour when the Tang Monk would arrive, the fiend used the kingdom’s wealth to erect the festooned tower. It meant to take him as a mate, absorb the pure primal yang of his vital essence, and thereby become an immortal of the Supreme Unity.

p.src: At precisely three quarters past noon, Tripitaka and Pilgrim mingled with the crowd and drew near the tower. The princess had just lit incense and was praying to Heaven and Earth. Around her stood fifty or seventy rouged beauties and embroidering maidens, while a close attendant held the embroidered ball. The tower had eight exquisitely latticed windows. The princess swept her gaze about and, seeing the Tang Monk draw very near, took the embroidered ball and cast it with her own hand upon his head. The Tang Monk started in alarm. The ball knocked his Vairocana cap askew, and he hurriedly raised both hands to steady it. The ball went tumbling into his sleeve. Everyone atop the tower shouted together, “It struck a monk! It struck a monk!” Well! At the crossroads, the throng of traveling merchants and others surged noisily forward, all scrambling for the embroidered ball. Pilgrim gave a shout, bared and ground his teeth, hunched his waist, and displayed an awe-inspiring form thirty feet tall, revealing a hideous face. The people were so terrified that they stumbled and crawled away, not daring to come near; in an instant the crowd had scattered. Pilgrim then resumed his original appearance.

p.src: The embroidering maidens, palace women, and eunuchs great and small descended from the tower, bowed to the Tang Monk, and said, “Noble sir, noble sir, please enter the court to receive congratulations.” Tripitaka hurriedly returned their courtesies and helped them rise. Then he turned and reproached Pilgrim: “You ape! You have played another trick on me.” Pilgrim laughed. “The embroidered ball struck your head and rolled into your sleeve. What has that to do with me? Why blame me?” Tripitaka said, “How are we to deal with this?” Pilgrim replied, “Master, set your mind at ease and enter the court to see His Majesty. I will return to the posthouse and tell Eight Rules and Friar Sand to wait. If the princess does not insist on marrying you, well and good: exchange the travel rescript and leave. But if she is determined to take you as her husband, tell the king, ‘Summon my disciples; I must give them some instructions.’ When the three of us are summoned into court, I shall be able to distinguish the true from the false. This is our stratagem of using the marriage to subdue the fiend.” Having no alternative, the Tang Monk agreed. Pilgrim turned and went back to the posthouse.

p.src: The elder was surrounded by the palace women and escorted to the front of the tower. The princess descended, took his arm with her jade-white hand, and boarded the jeweled carriage with him. The ceremonial procession formed up and returned to the palace gate. A chamberlain had already gone ahead to report: “Your Majesty, Her Highness the Princess is leading a monk by the arm. The embroidered ball must have struck him. They now await your decree outside the Meridian Gate.” The king was deeply displeased by this report and wished to drive the monk away. Yet, not knowing the princess’s wishes, he could only suppress his feelings and command that they enter. The princess and the Tang Monk came below the Golden Throne Hall. Truly: A pair styled husband and wife cried, “Long live the king”; through two gates, the wicked and the righteous bowed and wished him endless years. When the ceremonies were complete, they were summoned into the hall. The king asked, “Monk, whence have you come, to be chosen by my daughter’s cast ball?” Prostrating himself, the Tang Monk replied, “This humble monk was sent by the emperor of the Great Tang in the Southern Continent of Jambudvipa to worship the Buddha and seek scriptures at the Great Thunderclap Monastery in the Western Heaven. As I carry a travel rescript for this long journey, I came especially to Your Majesty’s court to have it exchanged. As I passed beneath the festooned tower at the crossroads, I did not expect Her Highness the Princess to cast her embroidered ball and strike me on the head. I am a man who has left the household and follows a foreign faith. How could I dare become the mate of one so precious and nobly born? I beg Your Majesty to pardon my capital offense, exchange my travel rescript, and dispatch me swiftly to Vulture Peak, that I may see the Buddha, obtain the scriptures, and return to my homeland, where Your Majesty’s heavenly grace shall be remembered forever.” The king said, “You are a holy monk from the Eastern Land. Truly, ‘A marriage destined across a thousand miles is joined by a thread.’ My princess has now reached the age of twenty and remains unmarried. Since the year, month, day, and hour were all auspicious today, we erected the festooned tower and had her cast the ball to seek a worthy mate. As chance would have it, she struck you. Though I myself am not pleased, I do not yet know the princess’s mind.” The princess kowtowed and said, “Father, as the common saying goes, ‘Marry a fowl and follow the fowl; marry a dog and follow the dog.’ Your daughter had already made a vow. I fashioned this ball, announced my purpose to Heaven, Earth, and the gods, and cast it to let Heaven choose my marriage. Today it struck the holy monk. This must be a bond from a former life that has brought about our meeting in this one. How could I dare change my choice? I wish to take him as my husband and imperial consort.” Only then was the king delighted, and he immediately commanded the chief official of the Imperial Astronomical Bureau to select a date. Meanwhile, preparations were made for the dowry, and an imperial decree was issued to announce the news throughout the realm.

p.src: When Tripitaka heard this, he offered no further thanks, but merely pleaded, “Release them, release them.” The king said, “This monk is utterly unreasonable. With all the wealth of my kingdom, We would take you as Our imperial son-in-law. Why will you not remain here and enjoy it, but think only of fetching the scriptures? If you refuse again, I shall have the officers of the Embroidered Guard drag you out and behead you.” The elder was so terrified that his soul nearly left his body. Trembling, he could only kowtow and petition, “I am deeply grateful for Your Majesty’s heavenly favor. Yet our company consists of four, and my three disciples are still outside. Now that I must accept, I have not even had a chance to give them a word of instruction. I beg you to summon them here, exchange the travel credential, and let them depart promptly, so that the purpose of our journey west may not be thwarted.” The king granted his petition and asked, “Where are your disciples?” Tripitaka replied, “They are all at the Court of Receptions hostel.” An officer was immediately sent to summon the holy monk’s disciples, so that they might take the travel credential and continue west while the holy monk remained there as imperial son-in-law. The elder had no choice but to rise and stand in attendance. A poem bears witness to this:

p.src: Now after Pilgrim parted from the Tang monk beneath the festooned tower, he took two steps and laughed twice, then returned to the hostel in high spirits. Bajie and Sha Monk came to meet him and asked, “Elder Brother, why are you grinning so merrily? And why is Master nowhere to be seen?” Pilgrim replied, “Master has met with a joyous occasion.” Bajie said, “We have not yet reached our destination, nor have we seen the Buddha, obtained the scriptures, and returned. What joyous occasion could there be?” Pilgrim laughed. “Master and I had only reached the festooned tower at the crossroads when, by sheer coincidence, the princess’s embroidered ball struck him. Some palace maids, court ladies, and eunuchs then crowded him before the tower, and he rode into court in a carriage with the princess to be made imperial son-in-law. If that is not joyous, what is?” Hearing this, Bajie stamped his feet and beat his chest. “If I had known, I should have gone! It was all that lazy Sha Monk’s fault. If you had not stopped me, I would have run straight beneath the festooned tower. Had the embroidered ball struck old Pig, and the princess taken me for her husband, would that not have been splendid and delightful? So handsome, dashing, and well-made—what marvelous fortune and sport for everyone! How amusing it would have been.” Sha Monk stepped forward, wiped a hand across his face, and said, “Shameless, shameless! What a brazen mouth you have. You are like a man who buys an old donkey for three mace of silver and then boasts of what a fine mount it is. If an embroidered ball had struck you, they would think even burning papers that very night to send you away was too late. Would they dare bring your ill-omened self through the door?” Bajie said, “You black-faced fellow have no appreciation. Ugly I may be, but I still have a certain charm. As the old saying goes, ‘Coarse in flesh and hide, but sturdy in bone and frame—every man has some merit worth choosing.’” Pilgrim said, “Idiot, stop talking nonsense and pack the luggage. I fear Master may grow anxious and send for us; then we must enter the court and protect him.” Bajie said, “Elder Brother, you are wrong again. Master has become the imperial son-in-law and will make merry in the palace with the emperor’s daughter. He is not climbing mountains and trudging roads, meeting fiends and demons. What does he need your protection for? At his age, surely he knows what goes on beneath the bedclothes. Does he need you to go and lend him a hand?” Pilgrim seized him by the ear, raised his fist, and cursed, “You clumsy oaf whose lustful heart never dies! What filthy nonsense are you spouting?”

p.src: While they were still quarreling, the hostel warden came to report, “His Majesty has issued a decree and sent an officer to invite the three divine monks.” Bajie asked, “What exactly does he want us for?” The hostel warden replied, “The venerable divine monk was fortunate enough to be struck by Her Highness the Princess’s embroidered ball and has been chosen as imperial son-in-law. That is why an officer has been sent to invite you.” Pilgrim asked, “Where is the officer? Tell him to come in.” The officer entered, saluted Pilgrim, and after completing the courtesies dared not look up. He merely muttered to himself, “Is it a ghost or a monster? Is it the Lord of Thunder or a yaksha?” Pilgrim said, “You there, why do you hesitate instead of speaking?” The officer was so frightened that he trembled all over. Holding the imperial decree aloft in both hands, he babbled, “My princess invites you to meet her kin—my lord invites her kin to meet him.” Bajie said, “We have no instruments of torture here and will not beat you. Speak slowly and do not be afraid.” Pilgrim said, “Do you think he is afraid you will beat him? It is your face he is afraid of. Quickly pack up, shoulder the luggage, and lead the horse. We shall enter the court, see Master, and discuss what is to be done.” And so it was that:
